head: claude/mi76-register-merge-driver
title: registers: a row-aware merge driver — the conflict is a header scalar, not the rows (MI-76)
body:
**MI-76**, parent `WO-20260901-PHASE-C`. Session `session_015r4U4QhowTzXAmr5KQ6f8L`. ▶️ START posted: [#6927 comment](https://github.com/benbaichmankass/Metis-Insights/issues/6927#issuecomment-5512607484). **Draft — the manager merges, not me.**

## 0 · Why the registers did not get the work store's treatment

Answered before designing, as asked, and it is **not** `RC-BUILT-A-MECHANISM-THAT-ALREADY-EXISTED`. Measured from `--diff-filter=A`:

| File | Born |
|---|---|
| `operating-layer-schema-and-state-DESIGN.md` + sharded `objects/` | **2026-09-01 14:58** |
| `SESSIONS.json` | 2026-09-01 16:42 — **1h44m after** |
| `MANAGER-CHECKLIST.json` | 2026-09-02 00:36 — 9h38m after |
| `OPEN-PRS.json` | 2026-09-02 09:20 — 18h22m after |

The design doc states the lesson as a property of the **object store** — *"Concurrency → one file per **object**"* — never as a repo-wide rule about shared JSON. So three registers born in the next 18 hours, each solving an urgent handoff problem, each re-made the original mistake, and nothing in CI could notice. The lesson was scoped to a directory rather than to a shape.

## 1 · What I measured

`main` @`1b82ab7`. Adjacent register-touching commit pairs since 2026-08-26, classified by what each side actually touched (row ids diffed against each commit's own parent — no reconstruction, no bias):

| Register | pairs | row-contested | **header-scalar contested** | disjoint |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `MANAGER-CHECKLIST.json` | 39 | 12 (31%) | **29 (74%)** | 27 |
| `OPEN-PRS.json` | 12 | 6 (50%) | **8 (67%)** | 6 |
| `SESSIONS.json` | 23 | 2 (9%) | **14 (61%)** | 21 |
| `OPEN-ITEMS.json` | 65 | **23 (35%)** | 2 (3%) | 42 |
| `health-review-backlog.json` | 91 | 8 (9%) | 1 (1%) | 83 |

**The finding that decided this PR: the dominant conflict mechanism is a shared header scalar, not the rows.** `updated_at`/`as_of` is bumped by *every* writer, so any two concurrent writes collide on one line.

Confirmed against the live set, not just the aggregate — **PR #10815's entire conflict in `MANAGER-CHECKLIST.json` is one line**:

```
<<<<<<< ours
  "as_of": "2026-09-02T15:46:00Z"
=======
  "as_of": "2026-09-02T11:22:00Z"
>>>>>>> theirs
```

And #10822's single hunk is `main` appending rows MI-70/MI-75 while the branch edits MI-74 — **semantically disjoint**, textually adjacent because appends land next to the last row and both bump `as_of`.

Two corrections to the framing in my brief, both measured:

- `MANAGER-CHECKLIST.json` is the most-touched register (24 commits/12h), but it is **not** mostly row-contested — 74% of its conflicts are the scalar.
- `health-review-backlog.json` at 6.2 MB is **91% fully disjoint**. Size is not the problem, exactly as suspected.

⚠️ **I ran a second simulation (reverse-applying patches to reconstruct siblings) and discarded it.** Reverse-apply fails precisely when two changes overlap, so it silently selected the non-conflicting cases — 72 of 91 pairs discarded and 0% conflicts reported. It is biased by construction and none of its numbers appear above.

## 2 · The choice, and why sharding lost

**Chosen: a `.gitattributes` merge driver.** ~450 lines, zero consumer changes.

⚠️ **Sharding does not fix the majority case.** One-file-per-row leaves `as_of` in the container file, which every writer still bumps — so it leaves **61–74% of work-store-register conflicts exactly where they are**. That alone settles it. Beyond that:

- **12 consumers read these files.** The driver changes no format, so none of them change. Sharding rewrites all 12 plus `run_guards.py`'s register guards — and *"a shard that breaks the readers is worse than the conflicts it fixes."*
- **`OPEN-ITEMS.json` is not byte-reproducible.** A shard/re-assemble migration is the single riskiest operation available on it; the driver never rewrites the file wholesale.
- **`backlog_append.py::append_row`'s exact-serialisation round-trip** survives untouched, because the driver splices original byte spans.

Sharding remains the right answer if row contention rises — `OPEN-ITEMS.json` at 35% is the one to watch, and it is also the one with no append helper.

## 3 · Proof

**It resolves the real conflicts.** All four register conflicts among the 12 currently-open PRs, by real `git merge` with the driver installed:

| PR | register | plain git | with driver |
|---|---|---|---|
| #10815 | `MANAGER-CHECKLIST.json` | CONFLICT | **clean** |
| #10822 | `MANAGER-CHECKLIST.json` | CONFLICT | **clean** |
| #10780 | `health-review-backlog.json` | CONFLICT | **clean** |
| #10694 | `health-review-backlog.json` | CONFLICT | **clean** |

4 of 4, rows verified (no id lost, none resurrected), output valid JSON. #10822's merge diff is **4 insertions / 3 deletions** — not a reformat.

**It refuses what it must.** 16 tests pass. The refusal cases are the point:

- **divergent same-id ADD → REFUSE.** This is the case that bit: the previous resolver reported *"no id lost, none resurrected"* while dropping an edit, because base contained neither row so a base-scoped divergence check never looked. Tested explicitly.
- divergent same-id EDIT → REFUSE · delete-vs-edit → REFUSE (both directions)
- **delete + untouched → stays deleted**, never reseeded from base
- header divergence that is *not* a bookkeeping timestamp → REFUSE

**Losslessness: BYTE identity, not semantic.** `--check-round-trip` parses and reassembles each register and compares bytes:

```
OK  health-review-backlog.json   OK  OPEN-ITEMS.json   OK  MANAGER-CHECKLIST.json
OK  SESSIONS.json                OK  OPEN-PRS.json
```

Including `OPEN-ITEMS.json`, which mixes a literal em-dash with an escaped one and does **not** survive `json.dumps`. Splicing byte spans is what makes it safe.

**Consumers unchanged and proven.** All 13 invocations of the named consumers run identically on a **driver-merged** tree and on pristine `main` — `handoff_check`, `open_pr_record --strict`, `session_registry status`, `manager_lease`, `render_session_brief`, `render_due_list`, `check_open_items`, `check_wip_ceiling`, `backlog_append`, `backlog_search`, `constraint_readout`, all rc=0 on both.

**Guards:** `python3 scripts/ci/run_guards.py --base main` → **PASS 49 · FAIL 1**. The one failure is `layer-guard: lint-imports exited 127` — `importlinter` is not installed in this container. That is environmental; I am not claiming it as a pass. `ruff-lint` failed on my own files and is fixed.

## 4 · What I could NOT make executable — read this before merging

⚠️ **A merge driver is client-side. GitHub does not run it.** It works on local `git merge`/`git rebase`, and only in a clone that has run `scripts/ops/install_merge_driver.sh` once — git refuses to take an executable path from a tracked file, so this cannot be committed away.

**So this does not make a `mergeable_state: dirty` PR auto-mergeable on GitHub, and the six PRs sitting armed with auto-merge would still sit.** What it removes is the hand-resolution cost, which the brief identifies as the largest consumer of manager time. I would rather state the gap than let the driver read as a fix for auto-merge.

Two follow-ups I did not build, both yours to scope:

1. **A CI/workflow auto-rebase** that runs the driver server-side and pushes the result — the only way to reach GitHub-side auto-merge.
2. **Removing the `as_of` contention at the source.** The driver resolves it; it does not question whether a whole-file timestamp every writer bumps should exist. Deleting it would remove the majority of these conflicts outright, and no consumer above reads it as anything but bookkeeping. That is a register-schema decision, and I did not take it unasked — but on the measurement it is the highest-value change left.
